## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.92511.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.92511.3.sa2)

Summary:

The large-conductance Ca2+ activated K+ channel (BK) has been reported to promote breast cancer progression, but it is not clear how. The present study, carried out in breast cancer cell lines, concludes that BK located in mitochondria reprograms cells towards the Warburg phenotype, one of the metabolic hallmarks of cancer.

Strengths:

The use of a wide array of modern complementary techniques, including metabolic imaging, respirometry, metabolomics and electrophysiology. On the whole experiments are astute and well designed, and appear carefully done. The use of a BK knock out cells to control for the specificity of the pharmacological tools is a major strength. The manuscript is clearly written. There are many interesting original observations that may give birth to new studies.

Weaknesses: The main conclusion regarding the role of a BK channel located in mitochondria appears is not sufficiently supported. Other perfectible aspects are the interpretation of co-localization experiments and the calibration of Ca2+ dyes. These points are discussed in more detail in the following paragraphs:

(1) May the metabolic effects be ascribed to a BK located in mitochondria? Unfortunately not, at least with the available evidence. While it is clear these cells have a BK in mitochondria (characteristic K+ currents detected in mitoplasts) and it is also well substantiated that the metabolic effects in intact cells are explained by an intracellular BK (paxilline effects absent in the BK KO), it does not follow that both observations are linked. Given that ectopic BK-DEC appeared at the surface, a confounding factor is the likely expression of BK in other intracellular locations such as ER, Golgi, endosomes, etc. To their credit authors acknowledge this limitation several times throughout the text ("...presumably mitoBK...") but not in other important places, particularly in title and abstract.

(2) mitoBK subcellular location. Pearson correlations of 0.6 and about zero were obtained between the locations of mitoGREEN on one side, and mRFP or RFP-GPI on the other (Figs. 1G and S1E). These are nice positive and negative controls. For BK-DECRFP however the Pearson correlation was about 0.2. What is the Z resolution of apotome imaging? Assuming an optimum optical section of 600 nm, as obtained a 1.4 NA objective with a confocal, that mitochondria are typically 100 nm in diameter and that BK-DECRFP appears to stain more structures that mitoGREEN, the positive correlation of 0.2 may not reflect colocalization. For instance, it could be that BK-DECRFP in not just in mitochondria but in a close underlying organelle e.g. the ER. Along the same line, why did BK-RFP also give a positive Pearson? Isn´t that unexpected? Considering that BK-DEC was found by patch clamping at the plasma membrane, the subcellular targeting of the channel is suspect. Could it be that the endogenous BK-DEC does actually reside exclusively in mitochondria (a true mitoBK), but overflows to other membranes upon overexpression? Regarding immunodetection of BK in the mitochondrial Percoll preparation (Fig. S5), absence of NKA demonstrates absence of plasma membrane contamination, but does not inform about contamination by other intracellular membranes.

(3) Calibration of fluorescent probes. The conclusion that BK blockers or BK expression affects resting Ca2+ levels should be better supported. Fluorescent sensors and dyes provide signals or ratios that need be calibrated if comparisons between different cell types or experimental conditions are to be made. This is implicitly acknowledged here when monitoring ER Ca2+, with an elaborate protocol to deplete the organelle in order to achieve a reading at zero Ca2+.

(4) Line 203. "...solely by the expression of BKCa-DECRFP in MCF-7 cells". Granted, the effect of BKCa-DECRFP on the basal FRET ratio appears stronger than that of BK-RFP, but it appears that the latter had some effect. Please provide the statistics of the latter against the control group (after calibration, see above).

The revised version of the manuscript has incorporated my suggestions to a very reasonable degree, in several cases with new experiments. The details of these improvements can be found in the correspondence.

claims.claim: The conductance of both BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP was sensitive to the BKCa blockers paxilline and iberiotoxin.
claims.source: Importantly, the conductance of both channels was sensitive to the BKCa blockers paxilline and iberiotoxin, as treatment of the cells with both compounds resulted in PM conductance values comparable to those of native MCF-7 cells (Figure 1E and H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, J and K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by patch-clamp experimental data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: MMTV-PyMT WT cells exhibited significantly elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions.
claims.source: Analysis of the Fura-2 fluorescence emission ratio showed significantly elevated basal (Figure 2A) and ATP-elicited maximal [Ca2+]cyto responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of MMTV-PyMT WT cells was reduced to the BK-KO cell level in response to paxilline.
claims.source: Interestingly, the elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of WT cells was reduced to the BK-KO cell level in response to paxilline (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but not by iberiotoxin (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Iberiotoxin did not reduce the elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of MMTV-PyMT WT cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, the elevated basal [Ca2+]cyto of WT cells was reduced to the BK-KO cell level in response to paxilline (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but not by iberiotoxin (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which is a peptide-based pore-blocking toxin that cannot pass the PM (Candia et al., 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures and citation to published literature.

claims.claim: Ionomycin-based calibrations confirmed the observed differences in basal [Ca2+]cyto between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
claims.source: To validate the observed basal differences in [Ca2+]cyto, we additionally performed ionomycin-based calibrations by chelating intracellular Ca2+, followed by Fura-2 saturation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D - F). These experiments confirmed the observed differences in basal [Ca2+]cyto, with [Ca2+]cyto of 170.2±8.0 nM, 98.40±4.8 nM and 178.5±13.5 nM for MMTV-PyMT WT, and 102.3±4.9 nM, 96.49±3.3 nM and 114.9±4.3 nM for MMTV-PyMT BK-KO cells, under control conditions, or in the presence of paxilline or iberiotoxin, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ionomycin-based calibration experiments shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Both BKCa blockers reduced the basal [Ca2+]cyto in MDA-MB-453 cells.
claims.source: Subsequently, basal and ATP-elicited maximal [Ca2+]cyto transients were recorded in the human BCC line MDA-MB-453, where both BKCa blockers reduced the basal [Ca2+]cyto (Figure 2B)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Maximal [Ca2+]cyto in MDA-MB-453 cells was not altered by paxilline or iberiotoxin treatment.
claims.source: while maximal [Ca2+]cyto was not altered by these treatments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Ionomycin-based experiments confirmed the BKCa-modulation dependent reduction of [Ca2+]cyto in MDA-MB-453 cells.
claims.source: Again, ionomycin-based experiments confirmed the BKCa-modulation dependent reduction of [Ca2+]cyto (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), with [Ca2+]cyto of 110.7±8.0 nM, 64.1±4.8 nM and 78.2±13.5 nM under control, paxilline- or iberiotoxin-treated conditions, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ionomycin-based calibration experiments shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Expression of both BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP increased the maximal and basal [Ca2+]cyto in MCF-7 cells.
claims.source: These experiments confirmed previous findings with the other BCC lines, as the expression of both splice variants increased the maximal (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I) and basal [Ca2+]cyto (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Fura-2 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: [Ca2+]cyto in MCF-7 cells was 31.5±3.7 nM, 58.1±6.4 nM and 52,9±5.6 nM in MCF-7 control cells expressing RFP, or MCF-7 cells expressing BKCaRFP or BKCa-DECRFP, respectively.
claims.source: [Ca2+]cyto in MCF-7 cells was found to be 31.5±3.7 nM, 58.1±6.4 nM and 52,9±5.6 nM in MCF-7 control cells expressing RFP, or MCF-7 cells expressing BKCaRFP or BKCa-DECRFP, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ionomycin-based calibration experiments.

claims.claim: Expression of BKCa reduced [Ca2+]ER throughout all BCCs investigated.
claims.source: Throughout all BCCs investigated, expression of BKCa reduced [Ca2+]ER, potentially indicating that the channel was (i) functional in this cell compartment and (ii) involved in regulating the Ca2+ homeostasis of the ER.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor.

claims.claim: In MMTV-PyMT WT cells, [Ca2+]ER was restored by the cell-permeable BKCa inhibitor paxilline but not by the cell-impermeable iberiotoxin.
claims.source: In MMTV-PyMT WT cells, [Ca2+]ER was restored by the cell-permeable BKCa inhibitor paxilline (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1K) but not by the cell-impermeable iberiotoxin (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1L)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Both paxilline and iberiotoxin restored the [Ca2+]ER in MDA-MB-453 cells.
claims.source: while both inhibitors restored the [Ca2+]ER in MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Overexpression of both RFP-tagged BKCa isoforms in MCF-7 cells depleted the [Ca2+]ER.
claims.source: Accordingly, overexpression of both RFP-tagged BKCa isoforms in MCF-7 cells depleted the [Ca2+]ER (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the D1ER sensor shown in the figure.

claims.claim: In MMTV-PyMT WT as well as MDA-MB-453 cells, functional expression of BKCa reduced basal [Ca2+]mito.
claims.source: In MMTV-PyMT WT (Figure 2G) as well as MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 2H), functional expression of BKCa reduced basal [Ca2+]mito.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figures.

claims.claim: In MMTV-PyMT WT and MDA-MB-453 cells, basal and maximally elicited [Ca2+]mito peaks increased in response to paxilline but not iberiotoxin treatment.
claims.source: Interestingly, in these two BCC types, basal and maximally elicited [Ca2+]mito peaks increased in response to paxilline (Figure 2G and H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1M—P), but not iberiotoxin treatment (Figure 2G and H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1M—P).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figures.

claims.claim: In MCF-7 cells, basal [Ca2+]mito was only affected upon expression of the mitochondrially targeted BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP.
claims.source: Importantly, in MCF-7 cells, basal [Ca2+]mito was only affected upon expression of the mitochondrially targeted BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP (Figure 2I)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Neither BKCaRFP nor BKCa-DECRFP affected the maximal [Ca2+]mito in MCF-7 cells.
claims.source: whereas neither of the two isoforms affected the maximal [Ca2+]mito (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Q).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the 4mtD3cpV sensor shown in the figure.

claims.claim: ECAR measurements unveiled an increased basal ECAR of MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells.
claims.source: ECAR measurements unveiled an increased basal ECAR of MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Maximal ECAR, received upon FCCP injection, was elevated in MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells.
claims.source: Maximal ECAR, received upon FCCP injection, was elevated in WT compared to BK-KO cells (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Only paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment equalized basal and maximal ECARs between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, only paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment equalized basal (Figure 3B) and maximal ECARs (Figure 3C) between WT and BK-KO, suggesting that intracellular BKCa channels stimulate the glycolytic activity of BCCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: In MDA-MB-453 cells iberiotoxin treatment did neither affect basal nor maximal ECARs.
claims.source: Moreover, in MDA-MB-453 cells iberiotoxin treatment did neither affect basal (Figure 3D and E) nor maximal ECARs (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Paxilline increased basal and maximal ECAR in MDA-MB-453 cells.
claims.source: Contrary to MMTV-PyMT WT cells, however, paxilline increased basal and maximal ECAR in these cells (Figure 3E and F)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: MMTV-PyMT WT cells showed a higher basal and maximal OCR compared to BCCs lacking BKCa.
claims.source: Interestingly, the increased basal and maximal ECAR (Figure 3A–C) in MMTV-PyMT WT cells correlated with a higher basal (Figure 3H) and maximal (Figure 3I) OCR compared to BCCs lacking BKCa.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Paxilline treatment reduced the basal and maximal OCR of BKCa proficient MMTV-PyMT cells to the BK-KO level.
claims.source: Paxilline treatment reduced the basal and maximal OCR of BKCa proficient MMTV-PyMT cells to the BK-KO level (Figure 3H and I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Iberiotoxin did not affect the OCR of MMTV-PyMT WT cells.
claims.source: while iberiotoxin did not have any effect (Figure 3H and I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: In MDA-MB-453 cells, paxilline treatment increased the OCR.
claims.source: Again, in MDA-MB-453 cells, paxilline treatment had an opposite effect to the observations that were made in MMTV-PyMT WT cells, as paxilline treatment increased the OCR (Figure 3J–L)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Iberiotoxin treatment did not affect the OCR of MDA-MB-453 cells.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular flux analysis data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Single time-point LC-MS measurements confirmed the metabolic differences between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
claims.source: Single time-point measurements confirmed the metabolic differences between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells and further demonstrated that BKCa inhibition by paxilline directly affected the concentrations of these metabolites (Figure 3M–P).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS-based metabolomics data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: BKCa inhibition by paxilline directly affected the concentrations of lactate, pyruvate, asparagine, and glutamine.
claims.source: Single time-point measurements confirmed the metabolic differences between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells and further demonstrated that BKCa inhibition by paxilline directly affected the concentrations of these metabolites (Figure 3M–P).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS-based metabolomics data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: MMTV-PyMT and MDA-MB-453 cells responded differently to paxilline treatment in terms of metabolite concentrations.
claims.source: As observed before by the ECAR and OCR measurements, MMTV-PyMT and MDA-MB-453 cells responded, however, differently to paxilline treatment (Figure 3M–P).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS-based metabolomics data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: TMRM measurements unveiled a less polarized ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT WT cells compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions.
claims.source: These measurements unveiled a less polarized ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT WT cells compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin, equalized ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells.
claims.source: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin, equalized ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Identical results regarding ΔΨmito were obtained in MDA-MB-453 cells.
claims.source: Identical results were obtained in MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 4C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT cells was tightly dependent on the extracellular glucose concentration.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that ΔΨmito of MMTV-PyMT cells was tightly dependent on the extracellular glucose concentration ([GLU]ex) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Under high [GLU]ex conditions (25.0 mM), the difference in ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells disappeared.
claims.source: Under high [GLU]ex conditions (25.0 mM), the difference in ΔΨmito between MMTV-PyMT WT and BK-KO cells disappeared, as ΔΨmito increased significantly in WT and decreased significantly in BK-KO cells compared to low [GLU]ex (2.0 mM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TMRM fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: In MMTV-PyMT cells, glucose removal as well as ATP-synthase inhibition reduced [ATP]mito, albeit the effect was more pronounced upon [GLU]ex depletion.
claims.source: In MMTV-PyMT cells, glucose removal as well as ATP-synthase inhibition reduced [ATP]mito, albeit the effect was more pronounced upon [GLU]ex depletion (Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the mtAT1.03 sensor shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment reduced the glucose, and increased ATP-synthase dependency of MMTV-PyMT WT cells for maintaining [ATP]mito.
claims.source: Remarkably, paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment reduced the glucose, and increased ATP-synthase dependency of MMTV-PyMT WT cells for maintaining [ATP]mito (Figure 4E and F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the mtAT1.03 sensor shown in the figures.

claims.claim: MDA-MB-453 cells showed an overall higher dependency on the ATP-synthase compared to MMTV-PyMT cells.
claims.source: These observations were confirmed in MDA-MB-453 cells, even though (i) these cells showed an overall higher dependency on the ATP-synthase, and (ii) the paxilline-sensitivity of [ATP]mito maintenance was much less pronounced (Figure 4G and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the mtAT1.03 sensor shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Expression of BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP, resulted in a high dependency on [GLU]ex to maintain [ATP]mito in MCF-7 cells.
claims.source: Expression of BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP, resulted in a high dependency on [GLU]ex to maintain [ATP]mito while the [ATP]mito rundown in the presence of Oligomycin-A was identical for both BKCa splice variants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the mtAT1.03 sensor in MCF-7 cells.

claims.claim: The [ATP]mito rundown in the presence of Oligomycin-A was identical for both BKCaRFP and BKCa-DECRFP in MCF-7 cells.
claims.source: Expression of BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP, resulted in a high dependency on [GLU]ex to maintain [ATP]mito while the [ATP]mito rundown in the presence of Oligomycin-A was identical for both BKCa splice variants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FRET-based imaging data using the mtAT1.03 sensor in MCF-7 cells.

claims.claim: MMTV-PyMT WT and MDA-MB-453 cells showed increased levels of [H2O2]mito.
claims.source: These experiments demonstrated increased levels of [H2O2]mito in MMTV-PyMT WT (Figure 4K) and MDA-MB-453 cells (Figure 4L)

claims.claim: BKCa-DECRFP expression in MCF-7 cells increased [H2O2]mito.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mitoHyPer3 fluorescence imaging data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: MMTV-PyMT BK-KO cells showed a higher rate of glucose uptake and phosphorylation compared to WT cells under basal conditions.

claims.claim: FCCP treatment increased 2-NBDG uptake in MMTV-PyMT WT and reduced uptake in BK-KO cells upon mitochondrial depolarization.

claims.claim: Mitochondria are less effective in assisting 2-NBDG uptake and phosphorylation in MMTV-PyMT WT cells, while they 'support' these processes in BK-KO cells under control conditions.

claims.claim: Paxilline treatment shifted the activity of the ATP-synthase to the ATP-supplying 'forward' mode in MMTV-PyMT WT cells.

claims.claim: Iberiotoxin treatment did not affect 2-NBDG uptake in MMTV-PyMT WT cells.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by 2-NBDG uptake measurements shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Paxilline treatment reduced basal accumulation of 2-NBDG in MDA-MB-453 cells.

claims.claim: In MDA-MB-453- and MMTV-PyMT WT-derived mitoplasts, channels of large conductance were detected.

claims.claim: For the channels detected in mitoplasts, the open probability did not significantly vary with the voltage.

claims.claim: The bursts of single-channel openings in mitoplasts showed an average conductance of 212±2 pS.

claims.claim: mitoBKCa was detected at a frequency of 6% in 127 mitoplast patches of MMTV-PyMT WT cells.

claims.claim: mitoBKCa was absent in 76 mitoplast patches from MMTV-PyMT BK-KO and 58 mitoplast patches from MCF-7 cells.

claims.claim: The molecular entity for the K+ channel derives from the nuclear Kcnma1 gene, which is ablated in the MMTV-PyMT BK-KO.

claims.claim: A protein band corresponding to BKCa was identified not only in whole-cell lysates, but also in isolated mitochondria.

claims.claim: The Na+/K+ ATPase was absent in the isolated mitochondrial protein fraction, confirming the purity of the mitochondrial preparation.

claims.claim: MMTV-PyMT WT cells exhibited an increased WI compared to BK-KO cells under control conditions.

claims.claim: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment reduced the WI in MMTV-PyMT WT cells to the BK-KO level.

claims.claim: The WI profiles of MDA-MB-453 and MCF-7 cells showed the same sensitivity towards paxilline.

claims.claim: In MCF-7 cells, the expression of BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP, stimulated the WI.

claims.claim: Cell treatment with siRNAs reduced the expression of BKCa or BKCa-DEC.

claims.claim: The knockdown of BKCa interfered with the WI in MMTV-PyMT and MDA-MB-453 cells.

claims.claim: BKCa-DEC-derived mitoBKCa channels stimulate the Warburg effect in BCCs.

claims.claim: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment, reduced the proliferation of MMTV-PyMT WT to the level of BKCa-deficient cells.

claims.claim: Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin treatment, reduced the proliferation of MDA-MB-453 cells.

results.result: BKCa-DEC splice variant localizes to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) of breast cancer cells. Electrophysiological characterization demonstrates functional BKCa channels in the plasma membrane of MMTV-PyMT WT and MDA-MB-453 cells, but not in BK-KO or MCF-7 cells. The BKCa-DEC isoform shows significantly higher mitochondrial colocalization than the canonical BKCa isoform in MCF-7 cells, with reduced plasma membrane currents compared to BKCaRFP despite comparable expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C44 provide converging electrophysiological and imaging evidence for functional BKCa expression at the plasma membrane and mitochondrial localization of BKCa-DEC. The differential localization of BKCa-DEC versus BKCaRFP (C40-C43) is supported by confocal imaging and patch-clamp data showing reduced PM currents for BKCa-DEC. The pharmacological sensitivity to paxilline and iberiotoxin (C30, C44) validates channel identity.

results.result: BKCa modulates subcellular Ca2+ homeostasis in breast cancer cells. Functional BKCa expression increases basal [Ca2+]cyto and reduces [Ca2+]ER and [Ca2+]mito. The effects show differential sensitivity to paxilline (cell-permeable) versus iberiotoxin (cell-impermeable), with [Ca2+]mito being exclusively sensitive to paxilline in MMTV-PyMT WT and MDA-MB-453 cells, and specifically affected by BKCa-DECRFP but not BKCaRFP expression in MCF-7 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C61 and C134-C144 provide comprehensive Ca2+ imaging data using Fura-2, D1ER, and 4mtD3cpV sensors across multiple cell lines and conditions. The differential sensitivity to paxilline versus iberiotoxin (C46-C47, C55, C59, C142) strongly supports intracellular BKCa localization. The isoform-specific effects in MCF-7 cells (C60, C143) further validate mitochondrial BKCa-DEC function. Ionomycin-based calibrations (C48, C51) confirm the observed differences.

results.result: Intracellular BKCa modulates metabolic activity in breast cancer cells. MMTV-PyMT WT cells show increased basal and maximal ECAR and OCR compared to BK-KO cells. Paxilline, but not iberiotoxin, equalizes these metabolic parameters between WT and BK-KO cells. LC-MS metabolomics confirms that paxilline affects concentrations of lactate, pyruvate, asparagine, and glutamine, though MMTV-PyMT and MDA-MB-453 cells respond differently to paxilline treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C74 are supported by extracellular flux analysis (Seahorse) and LC-MS metabolomics data. The consistent differential sensitivity to paxilline versus iberiotoxin across ECAR and OCR measurements (C64, C68-C69, C71) strongly supports the role of intracellular BKCa. The LC-MS data (C72-C73) provides direct metabolite measurements confirming the metabolic effects. However, the opposite effects of paxilline in MDA-MB-453 versus MMTV-PyMT cells (C66, C70, C74) suggest cell-type-specific metabolic contexts.

results.result: mitoBKCa depolarizes mitochondrial membrane potential and alters mitochondrial ATP production. MMTV-PyMT WT cells show less polarized ΔΨmito compared to BK-KO cells, which is equalized by paxilline but not iberiotoxin. Mitochondrial ATP maintenance is highly dependent on glucose in BKCa-expressing cells, with paxilline treatment reducing glucose dependency and increasing ATP-synthase dependency. BKCa-DECRFP expression specifically increases glucose dependency for [ATP]mito maintenance in MCF-7 cells. BKCa expression increases mitochondrial H2O2 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C86 and C147-C148 are supported by TMRM imaging for ΔΨmito and mtAT1.03 FRET sensor for [ATP]mito measurements. The consistent paxilline sensitivity without iberiotoxin effects (C76, C81) supports intracellular BKCa involvement. The glucose dependency data (C78-C79, C80-C81) and isoform-specific effects in MCF-7 cells (C83-C84) provide strong evidence for mitoBKCa function. The increased H2O2 levels (C85-C86) are consistent with mitochondrial stress. However, the mechanistic interpretation of reversed ATP-synthase activity (C148) is inferential and would benefit from direct measurement of ATP-synthase direction.

results.result: BKCa affects glucose uptake and ATP-synthase activity direction in breast cancer cells. MMTV-PyMT BK-KO cells show higher basal 2-NBDG uptake than WT cells. FCCP treatment increases 2-NBDG uptake in WT cells but reduces it in BK-KO cells, indicating that mitochondria are less effective in assisting glucose uptake in WT cells (ATP-synthase in reverse mode) while supporting it in BK-KO cells (forward mode). Paxilline treatment shifts ATP-synthase to forward mode in WT cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are supported by 2-NBDG uptake measurements under basal and FCCP-treated conditions. The opposite effects of FCCP on WT versus BK-KO cells (C88) provide strong evidence for differential ATP-synthase activity. The paxilline sensitivity (C90) supports intracellular BKCa involvement. However, the interpretation of ATP-synthase direction is indirect, based on the logic that FCCP-induced changes in glucose uptake reflect whether mitochondria supply or consume ATP. Direct measurement of ATP-synthase activity or ATP flux would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: Functional mitoBKCa channels are present in the inner mitochondrial membrane of breast cancer cells. Single-channel patch-clamp of mitoplasts from MDA-MB-453 and MMTV-PyMT WT cells detected channels with large conductance (~212 pS), Ca2+ sensitivity, and paxilline sensitivity, characteristic of BKCa. The channel was detected at frequencies of 15% in MDA-MB-453 and 6% in MMTV-PyMT WT mitoplasts, but was absent in BK-KO and MCF-7 mitoplasts. Western blot confirmed BKCa protein in isolated mitochondria with pure preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C102 provide direct electrophysiological evidence for mitoBKCa. The single-channel conductance (C95), pharmacological properties (C96), and absence in BK-KO cells (C99) strongly support the identity as BKCa derived from the Kcnma1 gene. The western blot data (C101-C102) confirms protein presence in purified mitochondria. The detection frequencies (C97-C98) are relatively low but consistent with the low BKCa-DEC expression in patient samples. The voltage-independence of open probability (C94) differs from plasma membrane BKCa, which may reflect the mitochondrial environment or channel modulation.

results.result: mitoBKCa stimulates the Warburg effect in breast cancer cells. MMTV-PyMT WT cells show increased Warburg index (WI) compared to BK-KO cells, which is reduced by paxilline but not iberiotoxin. MDA-MB-453 and MCF-7 cells show similar paxilline sensitivity. BKCa-DECRFP, but not BKCaRFP, stimulates WI in MCF-7 cells. siRNA knockdown of BKCa or specifically BKCa-DEC reduces WI in MMTV-PyMT and MDA-MB-453 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C110, C121, and C149 are supported by Laconic FRET-based lactate measurements. The differential sensitivity to paxilline versus iberiotoxin (C104) supports intracellular BKCa involvement. The isoform-specific effect in MCF-7 cells (C106) and the siRNA knockdown experiments (C107-C109) provide strong evidence that BKCa-DEC-derived mitoBKCa specifically stimulates the Warburg effect. The qPCR validation of knockdown (C107) strengthens the interpretation. However, the Warburg index is a derived metric based on lactate accumulation rates under different conditions, and direct measurement of lactate secretion would provide additional validation.

results.result: mitoBKCa promotes breast cancer cell proliferation and hypoxic resistance. MMTV-PyMT WT cells proliferate faster than BK-KO cells, and paxilline but not iberiotoxin reduces WT proliferation to BK-KO levels. Similar effects are observed in MDA-MB-453 cells. Ki-67 immunofluorescence confirms the MTT data. Colony formation assays show increased hypoxic resistance of MMTV-PyMT WT compared to BK-KO cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 and C122 are supported by MTT assays, Ki-67 immunofluorescence, and colony formation assays. The differential sensitivity to paxilline versus iberiotoxin (C112-C113) supports intracellular BKCa involvement. The Ki-67 data (C114) provides independent validation of the MTT results, addressing the concern that MTT also reflects mitochondrial function. The colony formation assays (C115) demonstrate functional consequences under hypoxic conditions. However, the proliferation assays measure population-level effects and do not distinguish between effects on cell division rate versus cell survival.

results.result: BKCa and BKCa-DEC transcripts are present in clinical breast cancer specimens. All 551 BC patient samples tested positive for BKCa mRNA expression, while 10 samples showed significant BKCa-DEC expression above the threshold. In BKCa-DEC positive samples, BKCa and BKCa-DEC expression levels are well correlated (R²=0.6060, p=0.008).
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118, C126-C127, C159-C160 are supported by nanostring mRNA expression analysis of 551 patient samples. The high prevalence of BKCa expression (100%) and low prevalence of BKCa-DEC expression (~2%) are clearly documented. The correlation between BKCa and BKCa-DEC expression in positive samples (C118) is statistically significant. However, the study is limited to hormone receptor-positive BC (C128), and the low abundance of BKCa-DEC may be underestimated due to bulk tumor analysis (C162). The lack of clinical outcome data (C163) limits the clinical interpretation.

results.result: mitoBKCa modulates overall cellular and mitochondrial energy production, mediates the Warburg effect, and promotes BC cell proliferation. These effects are sensitive to paxilline but not iberiotoxin, indicating that intracellular BKCa, presumably mitoBKCa, mediates malignant BCC behaviors. The observed alterations in subcellular Ca2+ homeostasis caused by BKCa have severe effects on cell metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C119-C120, C123-C125, C146, C167-C168 represent the main conclusions of the study, integrating evidence from multiple experimental approaches. The consistent differential sensitivity to paxilline versus iberiotoxin across metabolic, Ca2+ homeostasis, and proliferation assays strongly supports the role of intracellular BKCa. The combination of genetic (BK-KO, siRNA), pharmacological (paxilline, iberiotoxin), and overexpression (BKCa-DEC) approaches provides converging evidence. However, the inference that mitoBKCa is the primary mediator (C125) is based on the assumption that paxilline-sensitive, iberiotoxin-insensitive effects reflect mitochondrial localization, which is supported but not definitively proven by the localization and mitoplast patch-clamp data.

results.result: Targeting mitoBKCa could represent a treatment strategy for selected BC patients in future. BKCa may represent a novel anti-cancer treatment strategy for selected BC patients. The finding of BKCa-DEC in BC biopsies could be of considerable clinical relevance. mitoBKCa may ultimately be of clinical interest for new anti-cancer therapies.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C131, C161, C164, C169 are speculative statements about potential clinical applications. While the experimental data support the functional role of mitoBKCa in BC cell metabolism and proliferation, the clinical relevance is uncertain. The low prevalence of BKCa-DEC expression (~2% of samples, C160), the limitation to hormone receptor-positive BC (C128), and the lack of clinical outcome data (C163) limit the ability to assess clinical significance. Future studies correlating BKCa-DEC expression with treatment response and survival are needed (C164).

results.result: Background knowledge and prior work establish the context for the study. BKCa channels are implicated in cancer, particularly breast cancer. mitoBKCa has been identified in various cell types, including cardiac myocytes where the BKCa-DEC isoform forms functional channels. Cancer cells show metabolic reprogramming (Warburg effect) and increased energy demands. K+ and Ca2+ play important roles in cellular metabolism and cancer cell function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C8-C28, C130, C140, C145, C150-C153, C156-C157 represent background knowledge and prior work, supported by citations to published literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in the field. However, the accuracy of the cited work is not independently verified in this evaluation.

results.result: Study limitations and interpretations. The analyzed BC samples were all hormone receptor-positive, limiting generalizability. BKCa-DEC expression in BCCs appears less pronounced than in cardiac myocytes. The differential effects of intracellular versus plasma membrane BKCa on Ca2+ handling vary between cell types. The study design likely underestimates BKCa-DEC prevalence. The low detection frequency of mitoBKCa in patch-clamp experiments may reflect low channel abundance or limited mitochondrial expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129, C132-C133, C138, C141, C144, C154-C155, C162-C163, C165-C166 represent study limitations, interpretations, and comparisons to prior work. These claims are appropriately cautious and acknowledge limitations. The limitation to hormone receptor-positive BC (C128) is clearly stated. The comparison to cardiac myocytes (C132, C154-C155) provides useful context. The acknowledgment of potential underestimation of BKCa-DEC prevalence (C162) and the low patch-clamp detection frequency (C165-C166) are appropriate caveats.

results.result: Future work should investigate whether mitoBKCa directly contributes to lactate-induced tumor aggressiveness or extracellular K+ accumulation using live-cell imaging of extracellular metabolites in 3D BCC models.
results.evaluation: Claim C158 is a reasonable suggestion for future work based on the current findings. The study demonstrates that mitoBKCa promotes the Warburg effect and lactate production, but does not directly measure extracellular lactate or K+ in the tumor microenvironment. 3D models would provide a more physiologically relevant context. This is appropriately framed as future work rather than a current finding.

results.result: The authors claim that a BKCa splice variant (BKCa-DEC) localizes to the inner mitochondrial membrane (mitoBKCa) in breast cancer cells, supported by colocalization imaging, mitoplast patch-clamp recordings showing large-conductance K+ channels sensitive to Ca2+ and paxilline, and western blot detection of BKCa in isolated mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns about whether the metabolic effects can be ascribed to mitochondrial BKCa, noting that 'it does not follow that both observations are linked' and that BK-DEC appeared at the plasma membrane upon overexpression. The reviewer questions the colocalization data (Pearson correlation ~0.2) and notes that 'absence of NKA demonstrates absence of plasma membrane contamination, but does not inform about contamination by other intracellular membranes.' Reviewer 1 also questions the surprisingly low frequency of mitoBK-positive mitoplasts (6-15%) and asks how this affects interpretation. While reviewers acknowledge the patch-clamp evidence for a mitochondrial channel, they express uncertainty about whether this channel is responsible for the observed metabolic effects.

results.result: The authors claim that mitoBKCa modulates cellular metabolism, mediates the Warburg effect, and promotes metabolic reprogramming in breast cancer cells, based on ECAR/OCR measurements, metabolomics data, and Warburg index measurements showing differential sensitivity to paxilline (cell-permeable) versus iberiotoxin (cell-impermeable).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states that 'the main conclusion regarding the role of a BK channel located in mitochondria appears is not sufficiently supported' and notes that 'a confounding factor is the likely expression of BK in other intracellular locations such as ER, Golgi, endosomes, etc.' The reviewer acknowledges that 'it is clear these cells have a BK in mitochondria' and 'it is also well substantiated that the metabolic effects in intact cells are explained by an intracellular BK,' but emphasizes that 'it does not follow that both observations are linked.' The editor notes the study presents 'convincing evidence that an intracellular subpopulation of this channel reprograms breast cancer cells towards the Warburg phenotype,' but the specific attribution to mitochondrial BKCa remains questioned by reviewers.

results.result: The authors demonstrate functional BKCa channels at the plasma membrane of breast cancer cells using patch-clamp recordings showing paxilline- and iberiotoxin-sensitive K+ currents, membrane potential measurements, and cytosolic K+ concentration measurements.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these plasma membrane electrophysiology findings. Reviewer 2 notes 'the use of a BK knock out cells to control for the specificity of the pharmacological tools is a major strength' and acknowledges the experiments are 'astute and well designed, and appear carefully done.' The plasma membrane BKCa data serve as positive controls and are accepted by reviewers.

results.result: The authors report that BKCa expression modulates subcellular Ca2+ homeostasis in cytosol, ER, and mitochondria, with differential sensitivity to paxilline versus iberiotoxin suggesting involvement of intracellular BKCa pools.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical methodological concern: 'The conclusion that BK blockers or BK expression affects resting Ca2+ levels should be better supported. Fluorescent sensors and dyes provide signals or ratios that need be calibrated if comparisons between different cell types or experimental conditions are to be made.' Reviewer 1 asks about the rationale for using ATP to elicit Ca2+ signals and requests 'calibrated baseline values of Ca2+i.' While the authors added ionomycin-based calibrations in revision, the interpretation of differential effects on Ca2+ pools remains uncertain given the localization concerns raised by Reviewer 2.

results.result: The authors claim that mitoBKCa depolarizes mitochondria, increases glucose dependency, reverses ATP-synthase activity, and increases mitochondrial ROS production, based on TMRM measurements, mitochondrial ATP sensor data, mitoHyPer3 measurements, and 2-NBDG uptake assays.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions the mitochondrial potential measurement approach, asking 'Why did the authors use such a long time course and preincubated cells mit channel blockers overnight? Why did they not perform paired experiments and record the immediate effect of the BK channel blockers in the mito potential?' Reviewer 2's overarching concern about whether effects can be attributed to mitochondrial BKCa applies here as well. While the data show metabolic changes with paxilline treatment, the specific role of mitoBKCa versus other intracellular BKCa pools remains uncertain.

results.result: The authors claim that mitoBKCa promotes breast cancer cell proliferation under normoxic and hypoxic conditions, based on MTT assays, Ki-67 immunofluorescence, and colony formation assays showing differential sensitivity to paxilline versus iberiotoxin.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises an important concern: 'MTT assay are also based on mitochondrial function - since modulation of mito function is at the core of this manuscript, an alternative method should be used.' The authors added Ki-67 staining in revision, which Reviewer 1 acknowledges satisfactorily addresses this concern. However, Reviewer 2's broader concern about attributing effects to mitochondrial versus other intracellular BKCa pools applies to the proliferation data as well. The revised version appears to have addressed Reviewer 1's specific methodological concern, but uncertainty remains about the specific role of mitoBKCa.

results.result: The authors report detection of BKCa and BKCa-DEC transcripts in clinical breast cancer specimens, with all 551 samples positive for BKCa and 10 samples showing significant BKCa-DEC expression above threshold.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the nanostring expression data from patient samples. Reviewer 2 notes in the revised version that 'The revised version of the manuscript has incorporated my suggestions to a very reasonable degree, in several cases with new experiments.' The clinical expression data are accepted, though reviewers note limitations regarding the hormone receptor-positive patient cohort and the small number of BKCa-DEC positive samples.

results.result: The authors propose that targeting mitoBKCa could represent a treatment strategy for selected breast cancer patients, based on the functional and clinical data presented.
results.evaluation: The editor states this finding 'has potential therapeutic implications' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors also proposed that targeting mitoBKCa in combination with established anti-cancer approaches, could be considered as a novel treatment strategy.' While reviewers acknowledge limitations and call for future studies, they do not challenge the potential therapeutic relevance of the findings. This speculative claim about future therapeutic potential is accepted as reasonable given the data, though reviewers note the need for additional validation.

Peer reviewers SUPPORT the potential therapeutic relevance as reasonable speculation, acknowledging limitations but not challenging the therapeutic implications.
